Consider concurrent myocarditis (manage as myocarditis if present). rf Rechallenge Holding ICI is recommended for all grades of cardiovascular complications (ASCO); discontinue for >=G2. Appropriateness of rechallenge is unknown. rc G1 c1 Abnormal cardiac biomarker testing without symptoms and with no ECG abnormalities ICI Hold for G1 elevated troponin and recheck troponin 6 hours later; may resume once normalised or if believed not ICI-related. Treatment Consider myocarditis as a contributor; if myocarditis not present, manage as per usual pericardial-disease recommendations (NCCN defers to ESC / Adler 2015). [UNVERIFIED: NSAID + colchicine specifics are not stated in the ASCO/NCCN text.] Work-up + All grades warrant workup and intervention given the potential for cardiac compromise. ASCO 2021 · Table 9 (9.1 Pericarditis), G1 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_CARDIO-1 G2 c2 Abnormal cardiac biomarker testing with mild symptoms or new ECG abnormalities without conduction delay ICI Hold and discontinue for >=G2. Steroids Early (within 24 h) high-dose corticosteroids per the ASCO combined cardiovascular pathway: prednisone 1-2 mg/kg/day, oral or IV depending on symptoms. Treatment Consider myocarditis contribution; otherwise manage pericarditis per usual (ESC) recommendations. [UNVERIFIED: NSAID/colchicine dosing not specified in ASCO/NCCN text.] Work-up + Admit for cardiology consultation; echocardiogram to size the effusion. Referral Cardiology (cardio-oncology preferred). ASCO 2021 · Table 9 (9.1 Pericarditis), G2 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_CARDIO-1 G3 c3 Abnormal cardiac biomarker testing with either moderate symptoms or new conduction delay ICI Hold and discontinue. Steroids High-dose corticosteroids: prednisone 1-2 mg/kg/day (oral or IV); escalate to methylprednisolone 1 g/day if no immediate response (ASCO combined cardiovascular column). Escalation No response -> methylprednisolone 1 g/day + mycophenolate, infliximab, or ATG (infliximab contraindicated >5 mg/kg in moderate-severe HF). Work-up + Admit; transfer to coronary care unit if haemodynamic compromise or conduction abnormality. Referral Cardiology + ICU-level monitoring. ASCO 2021 · Table 9 (9.1 Pericarditis), G3 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_CARDIO-1 G4 c4 Moderate to severe decompensation, IV medication or intervention required, life-threatening conditions (includes tamponade) ICI Permanently discontinue. Acute Cardiac tamponade is an emergency -> urgent echocardiogram + cardiology; ICU. [UNVERIFIED: pericardiocentesis / pericardial drainage not spelled out in the ASCO/NCCN text; NCCN defers to the ESC pericardial-disease guideline (Adler 2015).] Manage decompensation per ACC/AHA with cardiology. Steroids High-dose / transplant-rejection-dose corticosteroids: methylprednisolone 1 g/day IV pulse for severe (ASCO combined cardiovascular column). Referral Cardio-oncology + ICU. ASCO 2021 · Table 9 (9.1 Pericarditis), G4 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_CARDIO-1

records.title: Encephalitis / aseptic meningitis
records.subtitle: irAE management · Neurologic
records.body: PD-1/PD-L1 · combo · CTLA-4 pd1 pdl1 combo ctla4 Encephalitis s9-encephalitis Aseptic meningitis s9-aseptic-meningitis Exclude EXCLUDE infection and CNS malignancy FIRST: bacterial/viral meningoencephalitis (HSV/VZV PCR, Gram stain, cultures) and CNS metastases / leptomeningeal disease (MRI + CSF cytology). Rule out concurrent anaemia/thrombocytopenia (can mimic with severe headache + confusion). Distinguish aseptic meningitis (NORMAL mentation) from encephalitis (altered mentation/behaviour, seizures). Baseline MRI brain w/wo contrast (+ pituitary/sellar protocol; + spine if indicated); LP - opening pressure, cell count/diff, cytology, protein, glucose, Gram stain, cultures, HSV/VZV + viral PCR, oligoclonal bands, autoimmune-encephalopathy + paraneoplastic panels; EEG (subclinical seizures) for encephalitis; AM cortisol + ACTH; ESR, CRP, ANCA, thyroid panel (TPO/thyroglobulin), GQ1b. Red flags Altered mentation, seizures, depressed consciousness, or focal deficit = encephalitis (treat aggressively); admit for G3-4. Start empiric IV acyclovir (10 mg/kg q8h) + antibacterial cover until infection excluded. rf Rechallenge Hold ICPi; discuss resumption only after weighing risks/benefits. NCCN: aseptic meningitis - hold if mild/moderate, consider discontinuing if severe; encephalitis - hold if mild, discontinue if moderate/severe. rc G1 c1 Mild: no functional interference. Any cranial-nerve problem is managed as G2 ICI Hold; discuss resumption only after weighing risks/benefits Antimicrobials Empiric IV acyclovir (10 mg/kg q8h) + antibacterial cover until CSF cultures and HSV/VZV PCR return negative Steroids Aseptic meningitis: once infection excluded, monitor OFF steroids or oral prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day. Encephalitis: trial IV methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day. Taper after 2-4 wk Referral Neurology consult ASCO 2021 · Table 7 (7.5 Aseptic meningitis / 7.6 Encephalitis), G1 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_NEURO-4 G2 c2 Moderate: some interference with ADLs ICI Aseptic meningitis: hold. Encephalitis: discontinue immunotherapy (NCCN, moderate/severe) Antimicrobials Continue empiric IV acyclovir + antibacterial cover until infection excluded Steroids Aseptic meningitis: oral prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day or IV methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day. Encephalitis: IV methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day; taper over 2-4 wk Escalation Encephalitis, if severe/progressing (over ~24 h) or oligoclonal bands: pulse IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day x3-5 days + IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days (0.4 g/kg/day) OR plasmapheresis Referral Neurology ASCO 2021 · Table 7 (7.5 Aseptic meningitis / 7.6 Encephalitis), G2 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_NEURO-4 G3 c3 Severe: limiting self-care and aids warranted ICI Aseptic meningitis: consider discontinuing (NCCN). Encephalitis: discontinue (NCCN). ASCO: hold, weigh risks/benefits Steroids Encephalitis: pulse IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day x3-5 days; taper over >=4-6 wk. Aseptic meningitis: IV methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day Escalation Encephalitis: add IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days (0.4 g/kg/day) OR plasmapheresis; rituximab if autoimmune-encephalopathy/paraneoplastic antibody positive or no improvement (NCCN: after 7-14 days) Work-up + Hospitalize (G3-4) Referral Neurology; ID team for encephalitis ASCO 2021 · Table 7 (7.5 Aseptic meningitis / 7.6 Encephalitis), G3-4 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_NEURO-4 G4 c4 Life-threatening consequences ICI Discontinue immunotherapy (NCCN: discontinue if moderate/severe; ASCO: hold, resume only after weighing risks/benefits) Steroids Pulse IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day x3-5 days; taper over >=4-6 wk Escalation IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days (0.4 g/kg/day) OR plasmapheresis; rituximab if antibody-positive or refractory Acute ICU-level inpatient care ASCO 2021 · Table 7 (7.6 Encephalitis), G3-4 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_NEURO-4

records.title: Guillain-Barre / peripheral neuropathy
records.subtitle: irAE management · Neurologic
records.body: PD-1/PD-L1 · combo pd1 pdl1 combo Guillain-Barre syndrome s15-guillain-barre-syndrome Peripheral motor neuropathy s15-peripheral-motor-neuropathy Peripheral sensory neuropathy s15-peripheral-sensory-neuropathy Exclude Other neuropathy causes before calling it irAE: chemotherapy, B12/B6/folate deficiency, diabetes (HbA1c), thyroid (TSH), paraproteinaemia (SPEP + immunofixation), Lyme, HIV, hepatitis B/C, paraneoplastic. CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, usually normal WBC in classical GBS); send cytology to exclude leptomeningeal disease, which can mimic GBS. Baseline Neurology consult; MRI spine w/wo contrast (+ brain if cranial-nerve involvement, + plexus if indicated); LP/CSF (cell count, cytology, protein, glucose, cultures); serum antiganglioside antibodies (anti-GQ1b = Miller Fisher variant); electrodiagnostics (NCS + EMG); PFT (NIF or VC); reversible-cause labs (HbA1c, B12, TSH, B6, folate, SPEP, CPK). Red flags Rapidly ascending / progressive weakness, respiratory compromise (monitor NIF/VC), bulbar signs (dysphagia, facial weakness), or autonomic dysfunction = GBS - admit with ICU access. Severe peripheral neuropathy may BE GBS and is managed as such. rf Rechallenge Peripheral neuropathy G2: resume once returned to <=G1. GBS / severe cases: extreme caution - rechallenge only after complete symptom resolution AND tapered off immunosuppression. rc G1 c1 Mild peripheral neuropathy - no functional interference (GBS has no G1); any cranial-nerve deficit is managed as G2 ICI Low threshold to hold and monitor symptoms for ~1 week; if continuing, monitor very closely for progression Treatment Observation; non-opioid neuropathic pain control (gabapentin, pregabalin, or duloxetine) if needed Work-up + Serum reversible-cause screen (B12, HbA1c, SPEP + immunofixation, HIV, ANCA); consider neuraxial imaging + neurology consult ASCO 2021 · Table 7 (7.3 Peripheral neuropathy), G1 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_NEURO-3 G2 c2 Moderate: some interference with ADLs (pain, no weakness/gait limitation). Progressive weakness = treat as GBS ICI Hold; resume once returned to <=G1. Progressive / GBS features: discontinue Steroids Initial observation OR prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day if progressing from mild; taper over 4-6 wk once IV methylprednisolone 2-4 mg/kg/day and manage as GBS Escalation Moderate GBS: IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days (0.4 g/kg/day) OR plasmapheresis (do NOT plasmapherese immediately after IVIG - it removes the immunoglobulin); steroids optional in idiopathic GBS but a trial is reasonable in ICI-related forms Treatment Gabapentin, pregabalin, or duloxetine for neuropathic pain Referral Neurology; inpatient with ICU access if GBS features ASCO 2021 · Table 7 (7.2 GBS / 7.3 Peripheral neuropathy), G2 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_NEURO-2/3 G3 c3 Severe: limiting self-care, weakness limiting walking or respiratory problems (foot drop, rapidly ascending changes) - manage as GBS ICI Permanently discontinue Steroids Idiopathic GBS is usually steroid-sparing, but a trial is reasonable in ICI-related forms: IV methylprednisolone 2-4 mg/kg/day; pulse methylprednisolone 1 g/day x5 days may be added for G3-4; taper over 4-6 wk. (NCCN: IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day x5 days, then taper over 4 wk) Escalation IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days (0.4 g/kg/day) OR plasmapheresis, alongside steroids Work-up + Frequent neuro checks + PFT (NIF/VC); monitor for autonomic dysfunction; treat constipation/ileus Referral Admit; inpatient with rapid transfer to ICU-level monitoring; neurology ASCO 2021 · Table 7 (7.2 GBS), G3-4 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_NEURO-2 G4 c4 Life-threatening (respiratory failure / dysautonomia) ICI Permanently discontinue Steroids IV methylprednisolone 2-4 mg/kg/day (or pulse 1 g/day x5 days) with taper over 4-6 wk Escalation IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days (0.4 g/kg/day) OR plasmapheresis Acute ICU-level care; ventilatory support if respiratory failure; monitor for autonomic instability ASCO 2021 · Table 7 (7.2 GBS), G3-4 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_NEURO-2

records.title: Myasthenia gravis
records.subtitle: irAE management · Neurologic
records.body: PD-1/PD-L1 · combo pd1 pdl1 combo Myasthenia gravis s15-myasthenia-gravis Exclude Overlap myocarditis + myositis (the 3 M's) - check troponin, CK/aldolase, ECG, TTE. Rule out CNS metastasis / leptomeningeal disease (MRI brain), and pneumonitis for respiratory symptoms. AChR-negative does NOT exclude MG - consider MuSK and LRP4 antibodies. Baseline Neurology consult. AChR + antistriational antibodies (add MuSK/LRP4 if AChR negative); PFT with NIF + VC; CPK, aldolase, ESR, CRP (concurrent myositis); troponin, ECG, consider TTE/cardiac MRI (concurrent myocarditis); EMG/NCS with repetitive stimulation +/- single-fibre EMG. Red flags Respiratory muscle weakness, bulbar signs (dysphagia, facial weakness), or rapidly progressive weakness = impending myasthenic crisis - monitor NIF/VC, admit (ICU-level). Concurrent myocarditis carries high fatality. Inpatient care may be appropriate even for initially mild cases. rf Rechallenge Hold at all grades. Resume ONLY in G2 (MGFA I-II) if symptoms resolve AND steroid taper completed; permanently discontinue for G3-4. Avoid drugs that worsen MG: beta-blockers, IV magnesium, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides. rc G2 c2 Some symptoms interfering with ADLs; MGFA class I (ocular only) or II (mild generalized weakness) ICI Hold; may resume only if symptoms resolve and steroid taper completed (NCCN: discontinue immunotherapy) Steroids Prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day PO - deliberately lower than 1 mg/kg, as high-dose steroid can transiently worsen MG; wean on improvement. (NCCN: start prednisone 20 mg/day, escalate q3-5 days to 1 mg/kg/day, max 100 mg/day, if no response; avoid >=2 mg/kg/day) Symptomatic Pyridostigmine 30 mg PO three times a day, titrate up to max 120 mg PO four times a day as tolerated Referral Neurology; strongly consider inpatient care - patients can deteriorate quickly ASCO 2021 · Table 7 (7.1 Myasthenia gravis), G2 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_NEURO-1 G3 c3 Limiting self-care; weakness limiting walking, ANY dysphagia, facial/respiratory muscle weakness, or rapidly progressive; MGFA III-V ICI Permanently discontinue Steroids Continue steroids; taper should begin 3-4 wk after initiation, then wean on symptom improvement. (NCCN: IV methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day) Escalation IVIG 2 g/kg IV over 5 days (0.4 g/kg/day) OR plasmapheresis x5 days; add rituximab if refractory (NCCN: 375 mg/m2 weekly x4, or 500 mg/m2 q2wk x2) Work-up + Frequent PFT (NIF/VC); daily neurologic review Referral Admit; may need ICU-level monitoring ASCO 2021 · Table 7 (7.1 Myasthenia gravis), G3-4 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_NEURO-1 G4 c4 Life-threatening (myasthenic crisis) ICI Permanently discontinue Steroids Continue steroids; taper begins 3-4 wk after initiation (NCCN: IV methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day) Escalation IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days (0.4 g/kg/day) OR plasmapheresis x5 days; rituximab if refractory Acute Admit; ICU-level monitoring for respiratory compromise/crisis; frequent PFT + daily neurologic review ASCO 2021 · Table 7 (7.1 Myasthenia gravis), G3-4 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_NEURO-1

records.title: Uveitis / ocular inflammation
records.subtitle: irAE management · Ocular
records.body: CTLA-4 · PD-1/PD-L1 · combo higher ctla4 pd1 pdl1 Uveitis s4-uveitis Exclude Infectious/other uveitis - syphilis, toxoplasmosis, TB (NCCN); evaluate + rule out before stopping ICI or starting local therapy. Rule out myasthenia gravis. Exclude patients with pre-existing active or recurrent uveitis needing systemic/continuous local therapy. Baseline Urgent ophthalmology referral for ALL grades: slit-lamp exam, visual acuity each eye, colour vision, red reflex, pupil size/shape/reactivity, intraocular pressure, dilated fundoscopy (+/- retinal nerve fibre layer, macular OCT per NCCN). Red flags Any visual compromise (vision urgent/emergent ophthalmology. Panuveitis can cause exudative retinal detachment and blindness. rf Rechallenge May resume once off systemic steroids (or prednisone <=10 mg/day) if ocular-only irAE and resolved to <=G1; topical/ocular steroids permitted on resumption. Permanently discontinue after recurrent events or a G4 presentation. rc G1 c1 Anterior uveitis with trace cells ICI Continue Treatment Artificial tears Referral Prompt ophthalmology referral (usually within 1 wk) ASCO 2021 · Table 10 (10.1 Uveitis), G1 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_OCUL-1 G2 c2 Anterior uveitis with 1+ or 2+ cells ICI Hold temporarily until after ophthalmology consult. NCCN: if stable on topical therapy, consider restarting in discussion with ophthalmology Treatment Topical corticosteroids (eg 1% prednisolone acetate) + cycloplegic (eg atropine); add systemic corticosteroids if needed Referral Urgent ophthalmology referral ASCO 2021 · Table 10 (10.1 Uveitis), G2 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_OCUL-1 G3 c3 Anterior uveitis with 3+ or greater cells; intermediate, posterior or pan-uveitis ICI Permanently discontinue (ASCO). NCCN: hold for posterior/pan-uveitis Steroids Systemic corticosteroids + intravitreal/periocular/topical corticosteroids. NCCN: prednisone/IV methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg/day) until <=G1, then taper over 4-6 wk Escalation Methotrexate if poor response to systemic steroids or severe sight-threatening inflammation; if refractory consider infliximab/other TNF-a blockers or IVIG Referral Urgent ophthalmology referral ASCO 2021 · Table 10 (10.1 Uveitis), G3 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_OCUL-1 G4 c4 Best-corrected visual acuity of 20/200 or worse in the affected eye ICI Permanently discontinue Steroids Systemic prednisone 1-2 mg/kg/day or methylprednisolone 0.8-1.6 mg/kg/day, plus intravitreal/periocular/topical corticosteroids per ophthalmology Escalation Infliximab/other TNF-a blockers or IVIG for severe, treatment-refractory cases Referral Emergent ophthalmology referral ASCO 2021 · Table 10 (10.1 Uveitis), G4 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_OCUL-1

records.title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
records.subtitle: irAE management · Haematologic
records.body: PD-1/PD-L1 · combo pd1 pdl1 combo Hemolytic anemia s0-hemolytic-anemia Hemolysis s0-hemolysis Anemia s0-anemia True Exclude Non-immune haemolysis - G6PD deficiency, drugs (dapsone, ribavirin, cephalosporins, penicillins, quinine), infection (mycoplasma, viral), TTP/HUS/DIC, PNH, MDS/bone-marrow failure. A negative DAT does NOT exclude ICI-AIHA (NCCN). Baseline CBC + peripheral smear (spherocytes, agglutination); reticulocyte count, LDH, haptoglobin, direct + indirect bilirubin, free haemoglobin; direct antiglobulin (Coombs) + cold agglutinin; PNH screen; G6PD; DIC panel. Monitor Hgb weekly until steroid taper complete. Red flags Rapid Hgb fall, transfusion need, cardiorespiratory compromise, or multi-lineage cytopenias -> urgent hematology/inpatient. Consider HLH if pancytopenia + very high ferritin. rf Rechallenge Hold from G2 and strongly consider permanent discontinuation for significant AIHA (ASCO). No data support restart after G3-4. rc G1 c1 Hgb <LLN to 10.0 g/dL (NCCN G1 = laboratory evidence of hemolysis only) ICI Continue with close clinical follow-up + lab evaluation (ASCO). NCCN: hold Steroids Not routinely indicated Work-up + Increased CBC + hemolysis-lab monitoring; rule out non-ICI causes ASCO 2021 · Table 8 (8.1 Hemolytic Anemia), G1 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_HEM-2 G2 c2 Hgb =2 g Hb drop, monitoring only, no transfusion) ICI Hold; strongly consider permanent discontinuation (ASCO) Steroids Prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day equivalents (NCCN 1 mg/kg/day); treat until Hgb stable off transfusion, then taper over 4-8 wk Referral Consider hematology ASCO 2021 · Table 8 (8.1 Hemolytic Anemia), G2 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_HEM-2 G3 c3 Hgb <8.0 g/dL; transfusion indicated (NCCN: hemolysis necessitating transfusion) ICI Permanently discontinue Steroids Prednisone 1-2 mg/kg/day (oral or IV per severity). NCCN: 1 mg/kg/day Escalation No response after 5-7 days -> add rituximab; then IVIG 2 g/kg (over 2-5 days), tacrolimus, cyclophosphamide, or mycophenolate mofetil Work-up + RBC transfusion per guidelines (minimum units; target 7-8 g/dL in stable noncardiac inpatients); folic acid 1 mg daily Referral Urgent hematology; consider inpatient care ASCO 2021 · Table 8 (8.1 Hemolytic Anemia), G3 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_HEM-2 G4 c4 Life-threatening consequences; urgent intervention indicated ICI Permanently discontinue Steroids IV (methyl)prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day Escalation No response/worsening after 3-5 days (or severe at presentation) -> add rituximab; then IVIG, cyclosporine, infliximab, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, tacrolimus, or ATG Work-up + Admit; RBC transfusion per guidelines Referral Hematology consult ASCO 2021 · Table 8 (8.1 Hemolytic Anemia), G4 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_HEM-2

records.title: Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
records.subtitle: irAE management · Haematologic
records.body: PD-1/PD-L1 · combo pd1 pdl1 combo Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis s8-secondary-hemophagocytic-lymphohistiocytosis Exclude Sepsis/infection (EBV, CMV), lymphoma or other malignancy-driven HLH, and other cytokine-release syndromes; ICI-related HLH-like findings may overlap CRS. Baseline Ferritin, fibrinogen, triglycerides, soluble IL-2 receptor (sCD25), CBC (cytopenias), LFTs, coagulation; calculate HScore; consider NK-cell activity; tissue biopsy (marrow/liver) for haemophagocytosis. Supportive: ferritin >=500 ng/mL, hypofibrinogenaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, transaminitis (NCCN, HLH2004-like criteria). Red flags Pancytopenia + high ferritin + fever + hepatosplenomegaly = emergency; high mortality if untreated -> urgent inpatient hematology. rf Rechallenge Hold ICI; resume only after full recovery with specialist input (IMMUNO-C). No established safe-rechallenge data. rc All grades c4 No agreed grading scale (NCCN); grade individual abnormalities (anaemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, liver enzymes) ICI Hold immunotherapy (high mortality; resume only after recovery + specialist input) Steroids Prednisone/IV methylprednisolone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day (or dexamethasone at equivalent dose); taper slowly (~10 mg/wk) titrated to response (ferritin, inflammatory markers) Escalation No response to steroids by day 5 -> add tocilizumab, anakinra, ruxolitinib, cyclosporine, or emapalumab-lzsg. Etoposide 150 mg/m2 IV twice weekly (wk 1-2) then once weekly for severe/refractory HLH (ASCO immunosuppressant appendix) Acute Inpatient care with hematology consult (high mortality if left untreated); consider consult with an HLH-like-syndrome expert NCCN v1.2026 ICI_HEM-4 · ASCO 2021 Table 8 has no HLH grading section (etoposide only, immunosuppressant appendix)

records.title: Immune thrombocytopenia
records.subtitle: irAE management · Haematologic
records.body: PD-1/PD-L1 · combo pd1 pdl1 combo Thrombocytopenia s0-thrombocytopenia True Exclude Other causes of thrombocytopenia - TTP, HUS, DIC, MDS, drug-induced, infection, HLH; check direct antiglobulin test to rule out concurrent Evans' syndrome (AIHA + ITP). Baseline CBC + peripheral blood smear + reticulocyte count; PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen; HIV/HCV/HBV/H. pylori; abdominal ultrasound (NCCN). Bone marrow only if other cell lines affected or aplastic anaemia suspected. Red flags Signs of bleeding (mucosal, GI, intracranial) or platelets urgent hematology + inpatient care. rf Rechallenge Hold and resume once recovered to <=G1 (IMMUNO-C). ICI not routinely permanently discontinued for isolated ITP. rc G1 c1 Platelets <LLN to 75,000/mm3 ICI Continue with close clinical follow-up + platelet monitoring Treatment None; monitor for signs of bleeding ASCO 2021 · Table 8 (8.6 ITP), G1 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_HEM-5 G2 c2 Platelets <75,000 to 50,000/mm3 ICI Hold; resume once recovered to <=G1 Steroids Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (range 0.5-2) orally ~4 wk, then taper over 4-6 wk to lowest effective dose. NCCN: start if no improvement within 4-6 wk Escalation IVIG with corticosteroids if a more rapid platelet rise is needed (NCCN: add IVIG 2 g/kg if bleeding) Referral Consider hematology ASCO 2021 · Table 8 (8.6 ITP), G2 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_HEM-5 G3 c3 Platelets <50,000 to 25,000/mm3 ICI Hold; interrupt until recovered to <=G1 Steroids Prednisone/IV methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day (NCCN); or dexamethasone 40 mg daily x4 days (ASCO alternative) Escalation IVIG 1 g/kg one-time (add if bleeding); if no response after 1-2 wk -> rituximab or thrombopoietin receptor agonists (romiplostim, eltrombopag) Referral Hematology consult; consider inpatient care ASCO 2021 · Table 8 (8.6 ITP), G3 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_HEM-5 G4 c4 Platelets <25,000/mm3 ICI Hold; interrupt until recovered to <=G1 Steroids Prednisone/IV methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day (IV per severity/speed of onset); or dexamethasone 40 mg daily x4 days Escalation IVIG 1 g/kg initial one-time dose; if refractory -> rituximab or thrombopoietin receptor agonists (romiplostim, eltrombopag) Referral Urgent hematology; inpatient care ASCO 2021 · Table 8 (8.6 ITP), G3-4 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_HEM-5

records.title: Infusion-related reaction
records.subtitle: irAE management · Infusion reactions
records.body: PD-L1 (avelumab highest) > PD-1/L1 > CTLA-4 lowest pd1 pdl1 ctla4 Infusion related reaction s10-infusion-related-reaction Cytokine release syndrome s8-cytokine-release-syndrome Exclude Distinguish from anaphylaxis/hypersensitivity and cytokine release syndrome; onset is typically during or shortly after the infusion. Baseline Vital signs, pulse oximetry during infusion; ECG if chest pain or sustained tachycardia. Avelumab (PD-L1) has the highest IRR rate (any-grade ~25%) - premedicate the first 4 infusions with acetaminophen + antihistamine per label. Red flags Hypoxaemia, hypotension, angioedema, bronchospasm, or chest pain -> stop infusion, manage as severe reaction/anaphylaxis, urgent intervention. rf Rechallenge After a severe reaction, switch to an alternate agent in the class (NCCN: PD-L1 -> PD-1) or rechallenge via desensitisation under allergist supervision (ASCO); premedication may prevent recurrence. rc G1 c1 Mild transient reaction; infusion interruption not indicated; intervention not indicated ICI Continue. NCCN: hold until symptoms resolve, then resume infusion as tolerated Treatment No intervention needed Premedication Consider acetaminophen + antihistamine (H1/H2) for subsequent infusions ASCO 2021 · Table 11 (11.1 IRRs), G1 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_INF-1 G2 c2 Infusion interruption indicated but responds promptly to symptomatic treatment; prophylactic medication indicated for <=24 h ICI Consider holding temporarily and/or reduce infusion rate to 50%; may resume/continue (NCCN: continue) Treatment Symptomatic - antihistamines, NSAIDs, opioids, IV fluids as clinically appropriate (per institutional guidelines) Premedication Prophylactic acetaminophen + antihistamine (H1/H2) for subsequent infusions; NCCN: consider corticosteroid premedication if prior reaction ASCO 2021 · Table 11 (11.1 IRRs), G2 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_INF-1 G3 c3 Prolonged (not rapidly responsive to symptomatic Rx and/or brief interruption); recurrence after initial improvement; hospitalisation for other sequelae ICI Hold; ASCO: may resume at 50% rate once <=G1. NCCN (G3-4): discontinue offending agent; consider an alternate agent in the therapeutic class Steroids IV corticosteroids + antihistamines (ASCO high-grade: cessation + IV corticosteroid + urgent intervention) Treatment Antihistamines, NSAIDs, opioids, IV fluids; hospitalisation for clinical sequelae ASCO 2021 · Table 11 (11.1 IRRs), G3 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_INF-1 G4 c4 Life-threatening consequences; urgent intervention indicated ICI Permanently discontinue Acute ICU-level inpatient care; IV corticosteroid + urgent intervention per institutional guidelines ASCO 2021 · Table 11 (11.1 IRRs), G4 · NCCN v1.2026 ICI_INF-1

ASCO Rec 1.2 low Low <10% Primary prophylaxis not indicated. Lowering the 20% threshold increases G-CSF use without improving outcomes. ASCO Rec 1.2 disc. After a neutropenic complication in a prior cycle (no primary prophylaxis given), where dose reduction or delay would compromise disease-free or overall survival. Otherwise dose reduction/delay is a reasonable alternative. Not for mobilisation. Avoid if <45 kg. Eflapegrastim-xnst long-acting 13.2 mg once per cycle SC ~24 h after chemo Not indicated for stem-cell mobilisation. Efbemalenograstim alfa-vuxw long-acting, non-pegylated per label, once per cycle SC after chemo Long-acting formulation (added NCCN MGF-B, v3.2026). Sargramostim GM-CSF 250 µg/m²/day Day of marrow infusion; ≥24 h after chemo, 12 h after RT Labelled for mobilisation, post-transplant, AML. Continue until ANC >1.5×10⁹/L ×3 days; reduce/stop if ANC >20×10⁹/L. Agents are equivalent in efficacy — choose by cost, convenience, availability. records.title: Antiemesis (CINV)
records.subtitle: Supportive care
records.body: Hesketh PJ, et al. Antiemetics: ASCO Guideline Update. J Clin Oncol 2020;38(24):2782-2797. DOI 10.1200/JCO.20.01296. Per-agent emetogenicity from NCCN Antiemesis v2.2026 (06/24/2026), classification tables — reworked for lookup, attributed to NCCN. Classify the regimen's emetogenicity, then give the matching prophylaxis. Emetogenicity = risk of emesis without prophylaxis; for combinations, use the highest-risk component. All checkpoint inhibitors are minimally emetogenic. high High — cisplatin & other high-risk single agents 4-drug: NK1-RA + 5-HT3-RA + dexamethasone + olanzapine (day 1) Continue dexamethasone + olanzapine days 2–4. ASCO · strong high High — anthracycline + cyclophosphamide (AC) 4-drug: NK1-RA + 5-HT3-RA + dexamethasone + olanzapine (day 1) Continue olanzapine days 2–4 (dexamethasone day 1 only in AC). ASCO · strong mid Moderate — carboplatin AUC ≥4 3-drug: NK1-RA + 5-HT3-RA + dexamethasone (day 1) NCCN classifies carboplatin AUC ≥4 as high emetic risk (so the lookup shows it as High); the NK1-containing 3-drug regimen is the same either way. ASCO · strong mid Moderate — other (excl. carboplatin AUC ≥4) 2-drug: 5-HT3-RA + dexamethasone (day 1) For agents that cause delayed CINV (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, oxaliplatin), may add dexamethasone days 2–3. ASCO · strong (delayed dex: moderate) low Low Single agent: a 5-HT3-RA OR dexamethasone 8 mg, before treatment ASCO · moderate min Minimal No routine antiemetic prophylaxis ASCO · moderate Combinations: give antiemetics for the component of greatest emetic risk. Lorazepam is a useful adjunct, not a single-agent antiemetic. Doses shown are ASCO; NCCN differs slightly (dexamethasone 12 mg for moderate risk, and a uniform 12 mg when paired with any NK1 antagonist). NK1 receptor antagonist Aprepitant 125 mg PO or 130 mg IV (day 1) 80 mg PO days 2–3 if oral aprepitant on day 1 NK1 receptor antagonist Fosaprepitant 150 mg IV (day 1) NK1 receptor antagonist Netupitant-palonosetron (NEPA) 300 mg netupitant / 0.5 mg palonosetron PO, single capsule Combined NK1 + 5-HT3 — no separate 5-HT3 needed NK1 receptor antagonist Fosnetupitant-palonosetron 235 mg / 0.25 mg palonosetron IV Combined NK1 + 5-HT3 — no separate 5-HT3 needed NK1 receptor antagonist Rolapitant 180 mg PO Pair with dexamethasone 20 mg day 1 5-HT3 receptor antagonist Palonosetron 0.50 mg PO or 0.25 mg IV 5-HT3 receptor antagonist Granisetron 2 mg PO or 1 mg / 0.01 mg/kg IV or 1 transdermal patch or 10 mg SC Patch / ER-SC cover multi-day 5-HT3 receptor antagonist Ondansetron High: 24 mg PO once or 8 mg / 0.15 mg/kg IV. Moderate: 8 mg PO BID or IV. Low: 8 mg PO or IV 5-HT3 receptor antagonist Dolasetron 100 mg PO only 5-HT3 receptor antagonist Tropisetron 5 mg PO or 5 mg IV 5-HT3 receptor antagonist Ramosetron 0.3 mg IV Corticosteroid Dexamethasone Day 1: 12 mg (with aprepitant/fosaprepitant/NEPA) or 20 mg (with rolapitant); Moderate 8 mg; Low 8 mg single If NO NK1 given: 20 mg day 1, 16 mg days 2–4. Days 2–4: 8 mg (see continuation per NK1 partner) Atypical antipsychotic Olanzapine 10 mg or 5 mg PO (day 1); same days 2–4 5 mg option if sedation is a concern Re-evaluate emetic risk, disease status, comorbidities and medications; confirm the regimen matches the emetic risk. ASCO · moderate If olanzapine was NOT given prophylactically → add olanzapine to the standard regimen. ASCO · moderate If olanzapine was already given → add an agent of a different class (NK1-RA, lorazepam/alprazolam, dopamine-RA, dronabinol, or nabilone). ASCO · moderate Prevent it: use the most active antiemetic regimen from the FIRST cycle rather than escalating after emesis occurs. If anticipatory nausea/vomiting develops → behavioural therapy with systematic desensitization; a benzodiazepine (lorazepam) may be added. ASCO · moderate High-dose chemo + stem-cell / BM transplant 3-drug: NK1-RA + 5-HT3-RA + dexamethasone (strong). A 4-drug regimen adding olanzapine may be offered (weak/new). Note: busulfan, melphalan, thiotepa are HEC in the HCT setting. ASCO Multiday antineoplastic therapy Give antiemetics appropriate to each day's emetic risk, continued for 2 days after the regimen ends. 4–5-day cisplatin: 3-drug NK1-RA + 5-HT3-RA + dexamethasone (strong). Granisetron patch / ER-SC covers multiple days. ASCO Checkpoint inhibitors Do NOT omit dexamethasone from a guideline-compliant regimen when a CPI is added to chemotherapy — no evidence it harms CPI efficacy. CPI alone or CPI + CPI is minimally emetogenic: no routine prophylaxis. ASCO Radiation-induced (RINV) High-risk RT (e.g. TBI): 5-HT3-RA + dexamethasone before each fraction + the day after. Moderate (upper abdomen, craniospinal): 5-HT3-RA before each fraction ± dexamethasone before the first 5 fractions. Low/minimal: breakthrough 5-HT3-RA, dexamethasone, or dopamine-RA (brain: breakthrough dexamethasone). Concurrent chemoRT: cover the higher of the two risks. records.title: Febrile neutropenia
records.subtitle: Supportive care
records.body: Taplitz RA, et al. Outpatient Management of Fever and Neutropenia in Adults Treated for Malignancy: ASCO/IDSA CPG Update. J Clin Oncol 2018;36(14):1443-1453. DOI 10.1200/JCO.2017.77.6211 (Table 2). ASCO Rec 2.1b · evidence-based, moderate Burden of febrile neutropenia (general clinical status) No or mild symptoms 5 Moderate symptoms 3 Severe symptoms or moribund Scores 5 / 3 / 0 are NOT cumulative — pick one. hypotension No hypotension (systolic BP > 90 mmHg) 5 copd No chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 4 tumor Solid tumor, or hematologic malignancy with no previous fungal infection 4 dehydration No dehydration requiring parenteral fluids 3 outpatient Outpatient status (at onset of fever) 3 age Age < 60 years 2 26 21 Score ≥ 21 → LOW RISK of medical complications — a candidate for outpatient management if clinical + psychosocial/logistic criteria are also met. Serious complications still occur in ≤ 11% of low-risk patients. Score < 21 → HIGH RISK — manage as an inpatient with IV empiric therapy. Taplitz RA, et al. Outpatient Management of Fever and Neutropenia in Adults Treated for Malignancy: ASCO/IDSA CPG Update. J Clin Oncol 2018;36(14):1443-1453. DOI 10.1200/JCO.2017.77.6211. Fever Single oral temperature ≥ 38.3°C (101°F), or ≥ 38.0°C (100.4°F) sustained over 1 hour. Neutropenia ANC < 1,000/µL (< 1.0 × 10⁹/L). Severe neutropenia ANC < 500/µL (< 0.5 × 10⁹/L). Profound neutropenia ANC < 100/µL (< 0.1 × 10⁹/L). Protracted Neutropenia lasting ≥ 7 days. Assess within 15 min of triage; give the first dose of empirical antibiotics within 1 hour of triage. FN is an oncologic emergency — major-complication rate ≈ 25–30%, mortality up to 11%. ASCO Rec 1.1g–h · strong (empiric antibiotics) Initial workup — ASCO Rec 1.1 History + physical to identify infectious foci CBC + differential, Hgb, platelets; electrolytes; creatinine, BUN, lactate; LFTs (bilirubin, ALP, transaminases) ≥ 2 sets of blood cultures from different sites (peripheral + one CVC lumen if present) Cultures from other sites (urine, respiratory, CSF, stool, wounds) as indicated Chest imaging if lower-respiratory signs/symptoms Nasopharyngeal swab for influenza (± expanded viral panel in heme malignancy/HSCT) Psychosocial + logistic requirements for outpatient care — ASCO Rec 3.1 Residence ≤ 1 hour or ≤ 30 miles (48 km) from clinic/hospital Primary care physician or oncologist agrees to outpatient management Able to comply with frequent clinic visits Family member/caregiver at home 24 h/day Access to a telephone and transportation 24 h/day No history of noncompliance with treatment protocols Exclude from outpatient care even if MASCC ≥ 21 — ASCO Table 1 Cardiovascular Presyncope/syncope · accelerated hypertension · new/worsening hypotension · uncontrolled heart failure, arrhythmia, or angina · clinically relevant bleeding · pericardial effusion Hematologic Platelets < 10,000/µL · Hb < 7 g/dL or Hct < 21% · ANC < 100/µL expected ≥ 7 days · DVT or PE Gastrointestinal Unable to swallow oral meds · new/worsening diarrhea · melena, hematochezia, or hematemesis · abdominal pain · ascites Hepatic Aminotransferases > 5× ULN or worsening · bilirubin > 2.0 mg/dL or clinically relevant increase Infectious Clear anatomic site of infection (pneumonia, cellulitis, abdominal, abnormal imaging/cultures) · severe sepsis · antimicrobial allergy · antibiotics ≤ 72 h before presentation · intravascular catheter infection Neurologic Altered mental status/sensorium or seizures · CNS infection or noninfectious meningitis · spinal cord compression · new/worsening neurologic deficit Pulmonary/Thorax Tachypnea or hypopnea · hypoxemia, hypercarbia · pneumothorax or pleural effusion · cavitary lung nodule or active intrathoracic process Renal CrCl ≤ 30 mL/min, oliguria, or worsening renal function · new gross hematuria · urinary obstruction or nephrolithiasis · clinically relevant dehydration · electrolyte abnormalities, acidosis, or alkalosis needing intervention Other comorbidity Major organ dysfunction or clinical worsening · physically/medically frail · pregnant or nursing · need for IV pain control · fractures, injuries, or need for emergent radiation Not a comprehensive list — does not replace clinical judgment. (ASCO Table 1) Outpatient (low-risk) oral empiric therapy — ASCO Rec 5.1 Oral fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin OR levofloxacin) PLUS amoxicillin/clavulanate — or PLUS clindamycin if penicillin-allergic. Do NOT use this regimen if fluoroquinolone prophylaxis was already used before the fever. Fluoroquinolone monotherapy is NOT recommended as initial outpatient therapy. In settings of high ESBL / fluoroquinolone resistance → admit + carbapenem. First dose in clinic/ED/hospital after cultures drawn; observe ≥ 4 hours before discharge (Rec 4.1). Inpatient (high-risk) IV empiric therapy — ASCO Rec 1.1h (IDSA) Monotherapy with an antipseudomonal β-lactam — cefepime, a carbapenem (meropenem or imipenem-cilastatin), or piperacillin-tazobactam. Vancomycin is NOT part of the standard initial regimen — add only for suspected catheter/skin-soft-tissue infection, pneumonia, or hemodynamic instability. Do not routinely add an aminoglycoside or a gram-positive-targeted agent — no outcome benefit, more toxicity. Escalate for resistant organisms: MRSA → vancomycin/linezolid/daptomycin · VRE → linezolid/daptomycin · ESBL → carbapenem · KPC → newer β-lactam / polymyxin. Deeper inpatient/ID management is out of scope — see the Acute module / local ID guidance. Persistent fever — ASCO Rec 6.1 Low-risk outpatients who do NOT defervesce after 2–3 days of empiric therapy → re-evaluate for a new/progressing infection site and consider hospitalization. Also admit for: fever recurrence, new signs/symptoms, oral meds no longer tolerated, regimen change needed, presentation cultures turning positive, or a resistant species. CISNE (Clinical Index of Stable Febrile Neutropenia) is a second validated score (Rec 2.2) for solid-tumor patients on mild-to-moderate chemo who appear clinically stable; it reclassifies some MASCC low-risk patients as higher risk. Not offered as a calculator here — MASCC is the ASCO-endorsed tool. Taplitz RA, et al. Antimicrobial Prophylaxis for Adult Patients With Cancer-Related Immunosuppression: ASCO/IDSA CPG Update. J Clin Oncol 2018;36(30):3043-3054. DOI 10.1200/JCO.18.00374. Doses per NCCN Guidelines, Prevention and Treatment of Cancer-Related Infections, Version 1.2026 (03/11/2026), FEV-A/B/C + INF-6 (facts-with-attribution). Prophylaxis is for HIGH-RISK patients — those expected to have profound, protracted neutropenia (ANC < 100/µL for ≥ 7 days), e.g. most AML/MDS or HSCT with myeloablative conditioning. NOT routine for solid tumors. Generally not indicated when G-CSF effectively shortens the neutropenic period. antibacterial Antibacterial — fluoroquinolone High risk of FN or profound, protracted neutropenia (most AML/MDS or myeloablative HSCT). NOT routine for solid tumors; may be considered for solid tumor/lymphoma expecting profound neutropenia ≥ 7 days when G-CSF is not given. ASCO Rec 1.2 · high evidence, moderate Levofloxacin 500–750 mg PO or IV daily Ciprofloxacin 500–750 mg PO q12h (or 400 mg IV q8–12h) FDA 2016 warning: fluoroquinolones cause disabling tendon/muscle/joint/nerve/CNS effects — reserve deliberately. Selects for C. difficile, enterococci, and FQ-resistant/ESBL gram-negatives; rising resistance limits utility. Cefpodoxime is an alternative if FQ-intolerant/allergic. pjp Pneumocystis jirovecii (PJP) Regimens with > 3.5% PJP-pneumonia risk — e.g. prednisone-equivalent ≥ 20 mg daily for ≥ 1 month, or purine-analog therapy. Also consider with prolonged corticosteroids (> 20 mg/day for > 4 weeks) used to treat irAEs. ASCO Rec 2.2 · high evidence, strong TMP-SMX (preferred) 1 single-strength daily OR 1 double-strength 3×/week If TMP-SMX-intolerant Dapsone (check G6PD first), atovaquone, or pentamidine (aerosolized or IV) TMP-SMX also covers Toxoplasma, Nocardia, Listeria; monitor for renal impairment, myelosuppression, hyperkalemia; interacts with methotrexate. Continue PJP prophylaxis until recovery from lymphocytopenia. (NCCN INF-6) antifungal Antifungal — triazole or echinocandin At risk for profound, protracted neutropenia (most AML/MDS or HSCT), especially with grade III–IV mucositis. NOT routine for solid tumors. Mold-active agent where invasive aspergillosis risk > 6%; candidiasis risk > 10% → triazole/echinocandin. ASCO Rec 2.1 · intermediate evidence, moderate Fluconazole 400 mg PO/IV daily — yeast only, NO mold activity Posaconazole (mold-active) 300 mg DR tablet PO BID day 1 → 300 mg PO/IV daily Micafungin (echinocandin) parenteral mold/yeast alternative Fluconazole covers yeast but NOT mold — use a mold-active azole (posaconazole, voriconazole, isavuconazole) or echinocandin where aspergillosis risk is high. Late post-allogeneic SCT / GVHD → consider a mold-active agent (e.g. posaconazole). Azoles have major CYP drug interactions and QTc effects — review carefully. antiviral Antiviral (HSV / HBV) HSV-seropositive patients undergoing allogeneic HSCT or leukemia induction → nucleoside analog. Patients at high risk of HBV reactivation → nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor. ASCO Rec 3.1 (HSV, strong) · Rec 3.2 (HBV, moderate) Acyclovir (HSV/VZV) 400–800 mg PO BID Valacyclovir (HSV/VZV) 500 mg PO BID (preferred over oral acyclovir for VZV) HBV reactivation Entecavir or tenofovir (per HBV screening guidance) Yearly inactivated influenza vaccine for all chemo patients + household/HCWs (> 65 y → high-dose). (Rec 3.3) Precautions — ASCO Rec 4.1–4.2 Hand hygiene + respiratory/cough etiquette for all health-care workers (strong). Neutropenic outpatients should avoid high airborne-fungal-spore environments (construction/demolition, gardening/soil, renovation) (strong). NOT recommended (no benefit): neutropenic diet, protected environments, surgical masks, footwear exchange, nutritional supplements. Neutrophil count decreased s11-neutrophil-count-decreased True White blood cell decreased s11-white-blood-cell-decreased True Fever s6-fever Sepsis s9-sepsis

records.title: Anaemia / ESA
records.subtitle: Supportive care
records.body: Bohlius J, et al. Management of Cancer-Associated Anemia With ESAs: ASCO/ASH Clinical Practice Guideline Update. J Clin Oncol 2019;37(15):1336-1351. DOI 10.1200/JCO.18.02142 (Recs 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.2, 6). gates 1–3 ASCO/ASH Rec 1.1; counselling Rec 6 · NCCN ANEM-3 cia Anaemia is chemotherapy-induced — on myelosuppressive chemotherapy, no other identifiable/treatable cause palliative Cancer treatment is non-curative (palliative) in intent hb Haemoglobin has declined to < 10 g/dL counsel Thromboembolism and mortality / tumour-progression risks discussed (shared decision) All criteria met → an ESA MAY be offered (ESA or RBC transfusion, by patient preference). Use FDA-label dosing, correct iron, and target the lowest Hb that avoids transfusion (do not exceed 12 g/dL). One or more criteria not met → an ESA is NOT indicated. Evaluate and treat reversible causes, correct iron deficiency, and use RBC transfusion for symptomatic or high-risk anaemia. ESAs are NOT recommended in Curative-intent chemotherapy — e.g. early-stage breast cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma, non-Hodgkin lymphomas, testicular cancer, early-stage NSCLC, and small cell lung cancer (ASCO Rec 1.2; NCCN ANEM-3). Anaemia NOT caused by chemotherapy (ASCO Rec 2.1) — except lower-risk MDS (see below). Patients not receiving cancer therapy, or receiving non-myelosuppressive therapy (NCCN ANEM-3). Outside the chemotherapy treatment period — discontinue by ~6 weeks after chemotherapy completion (NCCN ANEM-A). Exception — lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes with serum erythropoietin ≤ 500 IU/L: an ESA may be offered even without concurrent chemotherapy (ASCO/ASH Rec 2.2). Detailed MDS management is out of scope — see the NCCN MDS guideline. Decision framework: Bohlius J, et al. ASCO/ASH ESA Guideline Update. J Clin Oncol 2019;37(15):1336-1351. DOI 10.1200/JCO.18.02142. Evaluation, iron-deficiency thresholds, ESA dosing/titration & safety figures per NCCN Guidelines, Hematopoietic Growth Factors, Version 3.2026 (12/05/25), ANEM-1…ANEM-B (facts-with-attribution). Render-verified 2026-07-16. Transfusion threshold: Carson JL, et al. Red Blood Cell Transfusion: 2023 AABB International Guidelines. JAMA 2023;330(19):1892-1902. DOI 10.1001/jama.2023.12914 (Rec 2 for haematologic/oncologic patients; Rec 1 for the cardiovascular-disease threshold). Evaluate — confirm chemotherapy-induced anaemia Evaluate when Hb ≤ 11 g/dL or ≥ 2 g/dL below baseline. (NCCN ANEM-1) First: reticulocyte count (corrected for degree of anaemia) + MCV Haemorrhage — consider upper/lower endoscopy Haemolysis — direct antiglobulin test, DIC panel, haptoglobin, indirect bilirubin, LDH Nutritional — iron panel (serum iron, TIBC, ferritin), B₁₂, folate Renal dysfunction — GFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m² Cancer treatment / drug-induced myelosuppression; hormone dysfunction (thyroid, adrenal, hypogonadism) Anaemia of chronic inflammation (CRP, ESR); inherited causes; secondary myeloid disorders / CCUS An ESA is only appropriate once the anaemia is confirmed chemotherapy-induced and reversible causes are treated (ASCO Rec 4). Chronic inflammation, and recent oral iron or non-fasting sampling, can falsely elevate ferritin and TSAT — fasting is preferred. (NCCN ANEM-1) Iron — assess and correct before/with an ESA Iron panel: serum iron, TIBC, serum ferritin (+ transferrin saturation, TSAT). If ferritin and TSAT are discordant, the low ferritin takes precedence. IV iron is more effective than oral and improves Hb response / reduces transfusion when given with an ESA. (NCCN ANEM-4) Absolute iron deficiency Ferritin < 30 ng/mL AND TSAT < 20% IV or oral iron; if no Hb rise by 4 weeks, treat as functional deficiency def Functional iron deficiency (on ESA) Ferritin 30–500 ng/mL AND TSAT < 50% IV iron together with the ESA func Possible functional deficiency Ferritin > 500–800 ng/mL AND TSAT < 50% Usually no iron; consider IV iron for select patients (individualise) poss No iron deficiency Ferritin > 800 ng/mL OR TSAT ≥ 50% No iron supplementation needed none ESA protocol — agents, dosing & titration Epoetin alfa (incl. biosimilar epoetin alfa-epbx) 150 units/kg SC 3×/week → 300 units/kg 3×/week; OR 40,000 units SC weekly → 60,000 units weekly Darbepoetin alfa 2.25 µg/kg SC weekly → up to 4.5 µg/kg weekly; OR 500 µg SC every 3 weeks (300 µg = equivalent for initial dosing) Darbepoetin alfa fixed dose — 100 µg weekly, 200 µg every 2 weeks, or 300 µg every 3 weeks Epoetin alfa — 80,000 units every 2 weeks or 120,000 units every 3 weeks Epoetin alfa, epoetin beta, darbepoetin alfa, and biosimilar epoetin alfa are considered equivalent in efficacy and safety (ASCO Rec 5). All given subcutaneously. The escalation dose is for no response after the initial 4 weeks (epoetin) / 6 weeks (darbepoetin). Target the lowest Hb sufficient to avoid RBC transfusion — do NOT exceed 12 g/dL. If Hb reaches the transfusion-avoidance level or rises > 1 g/dL in any 2-week period, reduce the dose by 25% (epoetin alfa) or 40% (darbepoetin alfa). (ASCO Rec 8; NCCN ANEM-A) No response = Hb rise < 1 g/dL and still < 10 g/dL after 4 weeks (epoetin) or 6 weeks (darbepoetin) → discontinue after 8 weeks. Also discontinue once chemotherapy ends — do not continue outside the treatment period. (ASCO Rec 9; NCCN ANEM-A) RBC transfusion — alternative to, or adjunct with, an ESA Restrictive strategy: for hospitalised adults with haematologic/oncologic disorders, transfuse when Hb < 7 g/dL (AABB 2023 Rec 2); use an 8 g/dL threshold if there is pre-existing cardiovascular disease (AABB 2023 Rec 1). Symptomatic (physiologic): sustained tachycardia, tachypnoea, chest pain, dyspnoea on exertion, lightheadedness, syncope, or severe fatigue preventing usual activity → transfuse per AABB. High risk (progressive Hb decline with recent intensive chemo/RT), or asymptomatic with cardiac, chronic pulmonary, or cerebrovascular disease → consider transfusion per AABB. Asymptomatic without significant comorbidities → observe with periodic re-evaluation. (NCCN ANEM-2) ESA safety — weigh against transfusion, counsel every patient Thromboembolism ↑ — relative risk of thrombosis +48% to +69%; absolute VTE 7.5% (ESA) vs 4.9% (control). Evaluate risk factors: prior thromboembolism, heritable thrombophilia/hypercoagulability, elevated pre-chemo platelets, hypertension, steroids, prolonged immobilisation, recent surgery, IMiD-based myeloma therapy, hormonal agents. (NCCN ANEM-A; ASCO Rec 6) Survival / tumour progression — decreased survival when targeting Hb > 12 g/dL; the risk is not fully excluded even below 12 g/dL. Do not use outside the chemo treatment period or in patients not on chemotherapy. Possibly deleterious in metastatic breast cancer. Hypertension — control blood pressure before starting and monitor during treatment. Pure red cell aplasia (anti-EPO neutralising antibodies) — rare; suspect if a prior response to the ESA is lost, and report to the FDA. FDA boxed warning — ESAs are not indicated when the anticipated chemotherapy outcome is cure. Parenteral iron doses per NCCN Guidelines, Hematopoietic Growth Factors, Version 3.2026 (12/05/25), ANEM-B (facts-with-attribution). Render-verified 2026-07-16. IV iron (more effective than oral) improves Hb response and reduces transfusion when given with an ESA — 5 of 6 trials showed benefit in absolute or functional iron deficiency. Choose an agent by dose target and availability; total course ≈ 1000–1500 mg. Ferric carboxymaltose 750 mg IV (≥ 50 kg) ×2 doses ≥ 7 days apart, total 1500 mg; or 15 mg/kg IV (< 50 kg), max 1500 mg Severe hypophosphataemia — check phosphorus 5–10 days after dosing Ferric derisomaltose 1000 mg IV over ≥ 20 min, single dose (≥ 50 kg); or 20 mg/kg over ≥ 20 min (< 50 kg), max 1000 mg Ferric gluconate 125 mg IV over 60 min, once weekly × 8 doses (total 1000 mg); individual doses > 125 mg not recommended Ferumoxytol (select cases) 510 mg IV over 15 min ×2 doses 3–8 days apart (total 1020 mg); or 1020 mg IV single dose over 15–30 min For iron-deficiency anaemia if oral-iron intolerant/unresponsive or CKD; not prospectively studied in CIA; may interfere with MRI Iron sucrose 1000 mg total treatment course (various schedules — see prescribing information) Low-molecular-weight iron dextran Per prescribing information; test dose per institutional practice; IV (IM not recommended) Adverse effects may be delayed 24–48 hours Common IV-iron adverse effects: hypotension/hypertension, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, pain, fever, dyspnoea, pruritus, headache, dizziness. Premedication is NOT routine — reserve for a history of allergy to more than one drug, allergic diathesis/asthma, or inflammatory arthritis; give it before any test dose. Anemia s0-anemia True

records.title: Diarrhoea (CID)
records.subtitle: Supportive care
records.body: Bossi P, et al. Diarrhoea in adult cancer patients: ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines. Ann Oncol 2018;29(Suppl 4):iv126-iv142. DOI 10.1093/annonc/mdy145 (Table 1 warning signs; Table 10 general principles). ESMO 2018 Table 1 + Table 10 general principles [V, A] Grade the diarrhoea by CTCAE (increase in stools/day over baseline), then check for warning signs. ANY warning sign — or grade 3–4 diarrhoea — makes the course COMPLICATED and warrants admission and intensive treatment. g34 Grade 3–4 diarrhoea (≥ 7 stools/day over baseline, incontinence, or need for hospitalisation) fever Fever, sepsis or neutropaenic sepsis neutropenia Neutropaenia dehydration Dehydration — orthostasis, reduced urine output, or renal impairment cramps Moderate–severe abdominal cramping (especially not relieved by loperamide) nv Persistent nausea / vomiting (≥ grade 2), or inability to eat blood Frank blood in the stool ps Diminished performance status, or a previous admission for diarrhoea UNCOMPLICATED (grade 1–2, no warning signs) — manage as an outpatient: oral hydration + loperamide and dietary measures; reassess in 12–24 h. (ESMO Table 10 [V, A]) COMPLICATED — admit, give IV fluids/electrolytes, send a stool work-up including Clostridioides difficile, hold the offending drug, and treat intensively (± octreotide, consider empiric antibiotics); involve gastroenterology. (ESMO Table 10 [V, A]) Decision framework & doses: Bossi P, et al. Diarrhoea in adult cancer patients: ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines. Ann Oncol 2018;29(Suppl 4):iv126-iv142. DOI 10.1093/annonc/mdy145 (Tables 1, 2, 10). Agent-specific special-situation regimens (irinotecan, neratinib) from the current FDA prescribing information — see the Special situations section. Assess — grade, then triage uncomplicated vs complicated Grade by CTCAE Diarrhea (increase in stools/day over baseline; account for a stoma). Take a history: onset relative to the drug, culprit agent, stool frequency/consistency, blood, fever, oral intake. (ESMO Fig 1) Uncomplicated = grade 1–2 with no complicating signs → conservative outpatient management. (ESMO Table 10 [V, A]) Complicated = grade 3–4, OR grade 1–2 with any warning sign (moderate–severe cramping, nausea/vomiting, diminished performance status, fever, sepsis, neutropaenia, bleeding, dehydration) → hospitalise, evaluate, monitor closely, treat intensively; involve gastroenterology. (ESMO Table 10 [V, A]) WBC + differential — neutropaenia (febrile-neutropaenia risk) / leukocytosis (infection) Haemoglobin — blood loss / marrow; haemoconcentration Potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium — electrolyte disturbance Creatinine, urea — renal impairment CRP, procalcitonin — infection / inflammation Blood gases + lactate — acidosis (→ intensive care) Stool studies incl. Clostridioides difficile (also Salmonella, Campylobacter) — infective causes TSH / ACTH — rare endocrine causes (hyperthyroidism, hypoadrenalism) First-line — uncomplicated diarrhoea Loperamide — 4 mg initially, then 2 mg every 2–4 h or after every unformed stool; maximum 16 mg/day. (ESMO Table 10 [II, B]) Avoid spices, coffee, alcohol; reduce insoluble-fibre intake. (ESMO [V, C]) Avoid milk and dairy — except yogurt and firm cheeses — during the diarrhoea. (ESMO [V, C]) Small, frequent meals; oral rehydration solution between meals. Oral rehydration therapy for mild diarrhoea; an oral rehydration solution (WHO or commercial) for more severe disease. (ESMO [I–II, A]) Reassess at 12–24 h. If diarrhoea persists beyond 24–48 h on loperamide, or any warning sign develops, treat as complicated / refractory. Refractory or complicated diarrhoea IV fluids/electrolytes — rate must exceed ongoing losses (urine output + insensible ~30–50 mL/h + GI losses). If tachycardic/potentially septic, give an initial 20 mL/kg bolus; target urine output > 0.5 mL/kg/h. (ESMO Table 10 [I, A]) Oliguric AKI despite resuscitation → urgent intensive-care/nephrology input. (ESMO [V, B]) Octreotide — for diarrhoea refractory to loperamide or with severe toxicity: 100–150 µg s.c./i.v. three times daily, titrated up to 500 µg s.c./i.v. tid, or 25–50 µg/h by continuous i.v. infusion. (ESMO Table 10 [IV–V, B]) Other opioids — tincture of opium, morphine, or codeine — may be used. (ESMO [V, C]) Oral budesonide — an option for ChT-induced diarrhoea refractory to loperamide (ESMO [IV, C]); prophylactic budesonide is not recommended (ESMO [II, B]). Bile-acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam) — adjuvant for bile-salt malabsorption. (ESMO [III, B]) Consider empiric antibiotics (e.g. a fluoroquinolone) for complicated diarrhoea — fever, neutropaenia, or a positive/suspected infective work-up — after sending stool studies. Treat confirmed Clostridioides difficile per local infectious-disease guidance. Neutropaenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) — a distinct emergency Medical first line: broad-spectrum antibiotics covering gram-negatives, gram-positives and anaerobes (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam or imipenem-cilastatin, or cefepime/ceftazidime + metronidazole), plus G-CSF, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids, bowel rest, and serial abdominal examinations. Add amphotericin if no response (fungaemia is common). (ESMO [V, A]) AVOID anticholinergic, antidiarrhoeal and opioid agents — they may aggravate ileus. (ESMO [V, A]) Surgery for persistent GI bleeding, perforation, abscess, or clinical deterioration. (ESMO [V, A]) Safety — when NOT to reach for loperamide Immune-checkpoint-inhibitor colitis is managed differently — hold the ICI and give corticosteroids; loperamide/opioids are avoided in grade 3–4. Rule it out before treating diarrhoea as ordinary CID. (see the irAE lens → Colitis; ESMO Table 10) Neutropaenic enterocolitis — anti-motility and anticholinergic agents are contraindicated (ileus risk). (ESMO [V, A]) High-dose (irinotecan) loperamide — the 2 mg-every-2-h regimen is time-limited: not more than 48 consecutive hours, because of paralytic-ileus risk. (irinotecan label) Always exclude Clostridioides difficile and other infective causes before escalating anti-motility drugs, especially with fever, neutropaenia, or recent antibiotics. (ESMO Fig 2) Drug-specific regimens from the current FDA prescribing information (irinotecan, neratinib) and ESMO 2018 (fluoropyrimidines, infective, ICI). Each item is attributed. Some agents cause diarrhoea by a distinct mechanism or need a specific antidote or prophylaxis — these override the generic ladder above. Irinotecan Two patterns. EARLY / cholinergic (during or ≤ 24 h of infusion — cramping, diaphoresis, salivation, lacrimation): atropine 0.25–1 mg IV or SC, prophylactic or therapeutic (unless contraindicated). LATE (> 24 h; median onset ~day 5): high-dose loperamide — 4 mg at first onset, then 2 mg every 2 h until diarrhoea-free for ≥ 12 h (4 mg every 4 h overnight); do NOT exceed 48 consecutive hours (ileus). irinotecan FDA label (boxed warning; Warnings 5.1) Neratinib Diarrhoea is near-universal without prophylaxis (grade 3 in ~40%). Give mandatory loperamide prophylaxis from the first dose for 56 days: 4 mg three times daily (days 1–14), 4 mg twice daily (days 15–56), then 4 mg as needed (≤ 16 mg/day, titrate to 1–2 stools/day). A 2-week neratinib dose escalation is an alternative (grade ≥3 diarrhoea ~13%). Send stool cultures for grade 3–4 or complicated diarrhoea. neratinib (NERLYNX) FDA label, Table 1 EGFR / HER2 TKIs & other targeted agents Very common with EGFR/HER2 tyrosine-kinase inhibitors (afatinib 87–95% any grade, 14–22% grade 3–4; lapatinib); pertuzumab (a HER2 antibody), abemaciclib (a CDK4/6 inhibitor) and others also cause frequent diarrhoea. Manage with prompt loperamide + dietary measures and drug dose-modification; no drug-specific prophylaxis regimen is mandated (unlike neratinib). ESMO 2018 Table 5 Fluoropyrimidines (5-FU, capecitabine) Early, severe or life-threatening toxicity — including diarrhoea — within 96 h of 5-FU or capecitabine (including in DPD deficiency): uridine triacetate 10 g orally every 6 h for 20 doses, as an emergency antidote alongside supportive care. ESMO 2018 Table 10 [II, B] Clostridioides difficile / infective Test stool for C. difficile (and Salmonella, Campylobacter) — especially with fever, neutropaenia, or recent antibiotics. Confirmed C. difficile is treated per local infectious-disease guidance; do not miss it before escalating anti-motility drugs. ESMO 2018 Fig 2 Immune-checkpoint-inhibitor colitis NOT ordinary CID — hold the ICI and give corticosteroids; loperamide/opioids are avoided in grade 3–4, and infliximab/vedolizumab are used if refractory. Managed in the irAE lens (Colitis) — cross-check there before treating as chemo-induced diarrhoea. ESMO 2018 Table 10 · irAE lens (Colitis) Diarrhea s5-diarrhea

records.title: Oral mucositis
records.subtitle: Supportive care
records.body: Elad S, et al. MASCC/ISOO clinical practice guidelines for the management of mucositis secondary to cancer therapy. Cancer 2020;126(19):4423-4431. DOI 10.1002/cncr.33100 (PMC7540329). Palifermin schedule: Kepivance FDA label. MASCC/ISOO 2020 — setting-specific recommendations (strength · level of evidence) Pick the treatment setting → the MASCC/ISOO interventions recommended for THAT setting, each tagged with its recommendation strength. Every patient also receives basic oral care (below); these measures sit on top of it. melphalan High-dose melphalan — autologous HSCT Oral cryotherapy — ice chips held in the mouth around the melphalan infusion Recommendation II Photobiomodulation (intraoral low-level laser) — per a validated protocol Recommendation I hsct_tbi Autologous HSCT — high-dose chemo + TBI (haematologic) Palifermin — 60 µg/kg/day IV bolus ×3 days before + ×3 days after conditioning (6 doses); not with melphalan 200 mg/m² Recommendation I Photobiomodulation (intraoral low-level laser) — per a validated protocol Recommendation I hn_rt Head & neck RT alone (moderate-dose, < 50 Gy, no chemo) Benzydamine 0.15% mouthwash Recommendation I Photobiomodulation (intraoral low-level laser) — per a validated protocol Recommendation II hn_crt Head & neck chemoradiation (concurrent RT-CT) Photobiomodulation (intraoral low-level laser) — per a validated protocol Recommendation I Benzydamine 0.15% mouthwash Suggestion II Topical morphine 0.2% mouthwash — for established OM pain Suggestion III bolus_5fu Bolus 5-fluorouracil chemotherapy Oral cryotherapy — ice chips ~30 min during the 5-FU bolus Recommendation II other_chemo Standard-dose chemotherapy (other regimens) Multiagent basic oral-care protocol — no specific agent carries a further MASCC/ISOO recommendation in this setting Suggestion III Recommendations: Elad S, et al. MASCC/ISOO clinical practice guidelines for the management of mucositis secondary to cancer therapy. Cancer 2020;126(19):4423-4431. DOI 10.1002/cncr.33100 (PMC7540329). Palifermin schedule: Kepivance FDA label. mTOR-inhibitor stomatitis: everolimus (Afinitor) FDA label + SWISH trial (Rugo HS, et al. Lancet Oncol 2017;18(5):654-662, DOI 10.1016/S1470-2045(17)30109-2). Assess — grade the mucositis, flag the high-risk setting Grade by CTCAE Mucositis oral (symptom/functional bands). The WHO Oral Toxicity Scale is the classic OM-specific bedside scale — it combines the mucosal appearance with the ability to eat: 0 — none 1 — soreness / erythema, no ulcers 2 — ulcers, but able to eat solids 3 — ulcers, requires a liquid diet (cannot eat solids) 4 — ulcers, oral alimentation not possible (needs enteral / parenteral support) HSCT conditioning — high-dose melphalan, TBI, other high-dose regimens Head & neck radiotherapy, especially with concurrent chemotherapy Mucotoxic chemo — bolus 5-FU, high-dose methotrexate, anthracyclines, taxanes mTOR inhibitors (everolimus, temsirolimus) — a distinct aphthous-like stomatitis (see below) Basic oral care — the foundation for every patient A multiagent oral-care protocol (MASCC/ISOO suggestion for CT, H&N RT and HSCT) — the base on which the setting-specific measures sit. Dental evaluation and treatment before cancer therapy; patient education on oral care. Continue gentle toothbrushing and interproximal cleaning; do not stop brushing during neutropenia. Bland rinses — saline or sodium bicarbonate — for comfort and hygiene. Chlorhexidine is NOT recommended to prevent OM in head & neck RT (it does not reduce OM). Treatment of established oral mucositis — pain & support Topical morphine 0.2% mouthwash — MASCC/ISOO suggestion for OM pain in head & neck RT-CT. Systemic opioids for moderate–severe pain, including patient-controlled analgesia (morphine) in the HSCT setting — general supportive-care practice (doxepin mouthwash and transdermal fentanyl are not endorsed by MASCC/ISOO 2020 — no guideline possible). Nutrition and hydration support; escalate to enteral/parenteral support when oral intake fails (WHO grade 3–4). Look for and treat secondary infection — oral candidiasis, herpes simplex reactivation. mTOR-inhibitor stomatitis — a distinct entity Everolimus/temsirolimus cause an aphthous-like stomatitis (everolimus: 44–78%, grade 3–4 4–9%, usually within the first 8 weeks) that is NOT classic mucositis. Prevent it: start a dexamethasone alcohol-free oral solution as a swish-and-spit mouthwash when everolimus is started — SWISH regimen: 0.5 mg/5 mL, 10 mL, swish 2 min then spit, four times daily for 8 weeks (no food or drink for ≥ 1 h after); this cut grade ≥ 2 stomatitis to 2% vs 33% without it. Avoid alcohol-, peroxide-, iodine- or thyme-containing products. What NOT to use — MASCC/ISOO recommends against Sucralfate (combined topical + systemic) — recommendation against for prevention or treatment of OM pain in head & neck RT and solid-cancer chemo. Chlorhexidine mouthwash — suggestion against to prevent OM in head & neck RT. Antimicrobial lozenges/pastes — PTA (polymyxin/tobramycin/amphotericin B), BCoG (bacitracin/clotrimazole/gentamicin), and iseganan — recommendation against. Topical GM-CSF — suggestion against in HSCT. Parenteral (IV) glutamine — recommendation against in HSCT (higher relapse/mortality signal in one study). Pilocarpine and pentoxifylline — suggestion against; chewing gum — suggestion against in paediatric chemotherapy. Mucositis oral s5-mucositis-oral

records.title: CIPN (neuropathy)
records.subtitle: Supportive care
records.body: Agent-specific patterns & dose-modification from the FDA prescribing information and the ESMO-EONS-EANO 2020 CIPN guideline (Jordan B, et al. Ann Oncol 2020;31:1306-1319, DOI 10.1016/j.annonc.2020.07.003). FDA labels + ESMO-EONS-EANO 2020 Pick the neurotoxic agent → its CIPN pattern and the dose-modification / management approach. Managing the culprit drug is the single most effective lever — no agent prevents CIPN pharmacologically. oxaliplatin Oxaliplatin Two syndromes: an ACUTE, cold-triggered sensory neuropathy within hours–2 days (reversible, resolves in ~14 days, recurs each cycle; ~56% of patients) AND a delayed, cumulative sensory neuropathy (grade 3 median onset ~9 cycles adjuvant / ~6 advanced). Counsel cold-avoidance (no cold food/drink/air, gloves for the fridge; do NOT apply ice — it worsens the acute syndrome). Persistent grade 2 → reduce the oxaliplatin dose (75 mg/m² adjuvant, 65 mg/m² advanced); persistent grade 3 → discontinue. oxaliplatin FDA label; ESMO 2020 Table 5 cisplatin Cisplatin Cumulative large-fibre sensory neuropathy; may progress or persist for months after the platinum is stopped (‘coasting’); dose-limiting; also ototoxic. Reduce, delay or stop by grade and cumulative dose; warn that neuropathy can worsen after cessation. ESMO 2020; cisplatin label taxane Paclitaxel / taxane Length-dependent (stocking-glove) sensory neuropathy, sometimes an acute pain syndrome in the days after infusion; often partially reversible. Dose-reduce or delay for grade ≥ 2; consider switching to a less-neurotoxic taxane or reducing dose intensity. taxane FDA label; ESMO 2020 vincristine Vincristine / vinca alkaloid Dose-related sensorimotor neuropathy with prominent AUTONOMIC features (constipation, ileus); early loss of ankle reflexes. Reduce or hold for severe motor/autonomic toxicity. NEVER give intrathecally — it is almost always fatal (boxed warning). vincristine FDA label; ESMO 2020 bortezomib Bortezomib Predominantly PAINFUL sensory neuropathy (± autonomic); pre-existing neuropathy worsens. Give SUBCUTANEOUSLY and/or move to WEEKLY dosing — roughly halves neuropathy (grade ≥2 PN 24% SC vs 39% IV; grade ≥3 6% vs 15%). Grade 1 with pain or grade 2 → reduce; grade 3 → hold, then resume reduced; grade 4 → discontinue. bortezomib (Velcade) FDA label imid Thalidomide / IMiD Dose- and duration-dependent sensory neuropathy that may be irreversible. Reduce or stop for grade ≥ 2; monitor cumulatively; lenalidomide/pomalidomide are far less neurotoxic than thalidomide. ESMO 2020; thalidomide label Loprinzi CL, et al. Prevention and Management of CIPN in Survivors of Adult Cancers: ASCO Guideline Update. J Clin Oncol 2020;38(28):3325-3348. DOI 10.1200/JCO.20.01399. Cross-checked with ESMO-EONS-EANO 2020 (Jordan B, et al. Ann Oncol 2020;31:1306-1319, DOI 10.1016/j.annonc.2020.07.003), which supplies dosing and grades (LoE/GoR). Duloxetine titration and agent dose-modification cross-checked against the FDA labels and the ESMO 2020 treatment table. Assess — grade, and identify the culprit agent Grade by CTCAE Peripheral sensory neuropathy and Peripheral motor neuropathy (patient-reported symptoms + functional impact). Ask which neurotoxic agent, the pattern (sensory / motor / autonomic), the timing, and whether function or safety is affected. Culprit agents: platinums (oxaliplatin, cisplatin), taxanes, vinca alkaloids, bortezomib, thalidomide/IMiDs, eribulin. Mostly length-dependent sensory (numbness, tingling, pain); motor and autonomic involvement flag more severe or vinca/bortezomib neuropathy. ‘Coasting’ — platinum neuropathy can worsen for months after the drug is stopped. Oxaliplatin also causes a distinct acute, cold-triggered syndrome (see the agent selector). Prevention — the honest message No agent is recommended to prevent CIPN (ASCO 2020; ESMO-EONS-EANO 2020). Acetyl-L-carnitine should NOT be offered — it significantly WORSENED CIPN over 2 years (possible harm; ESMO LoE I, GoR E). The effective lever is managing the neurotoxic drug (dose, schedule, route) plus patient counselling; physical exercise may help but the evidence is weak. Acetyl-L-carnitine — discouraged; worsens CIPN (harm). Calcium/magnesium infusions (oxaliplatin) — not recommended (ESMO I, E). Glutathione, diethyldithiocarbamate (platinum) — not recommended (I, E). Vitamin E, vitamin B, alpha-lipoic acid, amifostine, omega-3, goshajinkigan, minocycline — insufficient/negative evidence. Amitriptyline, carbamazepine, nimodipine for prevention — not recommended. Treatment of established painful CIPN Duloxetine is the ONLY agent with evidence for painful CIPN — 30 mg/day for 1 week, then 60 mg/day (ESMO LoE I, GoR B); cisplatin-treated patients respond better than taxane-treated. Set expectations: the average benefit is limited. (ASCO 2020; ESMO 2020) Gabapentin (target ~2700 mg/day) or pregabalin (target 300 mg twice daily) — a dedicated CIPN gabapentin trial was negative, but they are established for other neuropathic pain; offer by shared decision. Nortriptyline (up to ~100 mg/day) or amitriptyline (start 10–25, target ~50 mg/day) — small/limited CIPN data. Topical compounded gel — baclofen 10 mg / amitriptyline 40 mg / ketamine 20 mg; or topical menthol 1% cream twice daily. Venlafaxine, tramadol or a strong opioid — as neuropathic-pain options / salvage, by shared decision. Physical exercise — the best-supported non-drug option (ESMO LoE II, GoR B). Acupuncture and scrambler therapy — emerging, limited evidence. Occupational-therapy fall-prevention and safety measures for sensory/motor deficits; refer for severe or refractory CIPN. Peripheral sensory neuropathy s15-peripheral-sensory-neuropathy Peripheral motor neuropathy s15-peripheral-motor-neuropathy Autonomic neuropathy s15-autonomic-neuropathy
