records.body: Rate pain intensity, establish opioid history, then select the matching scenario. Opioid-tolerant (FDA) = taking, for ≥ 1 week, ≥ 60 mg oral morphine/day, ≥ 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, ≥ 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, ≥ 25 mcg/h fentanyl patch, or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid; opioid-naïve otherwise. NCCN Adult Cancer Pain v2.2026, PAIN-2/PAIN-4/PAIN-5/PAIN-6 Naïve · mild Opioid-naïve, mild pain Foundation General principles apply throughout (PAIN-3); optimise disease-directed therapy. First step Non-opioids ± adjuvant analgesics first, unless contraindicated by adverse effects, drug interactions, or comorbidity. Then Add short-acting opioid only if pain is not controlled; if reached, follow the moderate/severe pathway. PAIN-4 (opioid-naïve). Naïve · mod/severe Opioid-naïve, moderate to severe pain Non-opioids Continue non-opioids and adjuvants as appropriate, with short-acting opioid as needed. Start (short-acting, q3–4h PRN) Morphine 5 mg oral solution, or IR 7.5 mg (half a 15 mg tablet); hydromorphone 2 mg PO; oxycodone IR 2.5–5 mg ± acetaminophen 325 mg; hydrocodone 5 mg with acetaminophen 325 mg. Frail / older Consider a half tablet for lower-dose titration. Alternative Buprenorphine (5 mcg/h transdermal patch every 7 days, or buccal film 75 mcg 1–2×/day) if more sensitive to full-agonist effects — note it can take hours–days to act, so treat severe pain with an IR opioid. Long-acting If multiple short-acting doses are needed each day, consider adding a long-acting opioid based on total daily dose and expected trajectory. If uncontrolled Reassess with a comprehensive pain assessment; consider radiation oncology, pain medicine or palliative care; consider opioid rotation for dose-limiting adverse effects. PAIN-4. Doses verified render-side. Tolerant · mod/severe Opioid-tolerant, moderate to severe pain Non-opioids Non-opioids and adjuvants as appropriate, with short-acting opioid as needed. Titrate Titrate the short-acting opioid — a dose increase of 30%–100% may be required. Long-acting If multiple short-acting doses are consistently needed per day, add or increase a long-acting opioid based on total daily dose and expected trajectory. If mild For mild pain, re-evaluate the need for opioids and reduce if appropriate. If uncontrolled Reassess the working diagnosis with a comprehensive pain assessment; consider specialty consultation and opioid rotation. PAIN-5. Pain crisis Severe uncontrolled pain / pain crisis — a medical emergency Oral (IR, peak ~60 min) Opioid-naïve: 5–15 mg oral short-acting morphine sulfate (or equivalent). Opioid-tolerant: an oral dose equal to 10%–20% of the total opioid taken in the previous 24 h. IV bolus (peak ~15 min) Opioid-naïve: 2–5 mg IV morphine sulfate (or equivalent). Opioid-tolerant: an IV dose equal to 10%–20% of the previous 24 h total. A subcutaneous bolus (peak ~30 min) can substitute for IV; PCA is an option. Reassess (60 min PO / 15 min IV) Pain unchanged or worse → increase the dose by 50%–100%. Pain reduced but inadequately controlled → repeat the same dose or increase by 25%. Pain adequately controlled → continue the current effective dose as needed over the first 24 h. After 2–3 cycles Move to the opioid-tolerant pathway (PAIN-5) and Ongoing Care (PAIN-7); consider inpatient / hospice admission to reach comfort and function goals. Titrate with caution in renal/hepatic impairment, chronic lung disease, airway compromise, sleep apnoea, or poor performance status. PAIN-6. Doses verified render-side. Assess — screen, quantify, set goals Screen for pain at every contact; the patient's self-report is the primary measure. Quantify intensity, location and quality, and perform a comprehensive assessment for new, worsening or persisting pain. Severe uncontrolled pain is a medical emergency. Analgesia — optimise pain relief Activities — optimise activities of daily living Adverse effects — minimise, and prevent constipation from the outset Aberrant behaviour — monitor for aberrant drug use; assess misuse/diversion risk Affect — address the relationship between pain and mood Manage persistent pain with regularly scheduled or long-acting analgesics, and breakthrough/incident pain with supplemental short-acting doses. Consider early referral to palliative care. PAIN-1 / PAIN-2 / PAIN-3 Non-opioid analgesics 650 mg every 4 h or 1 g every 6 h (daily maximum 4 g/day) with normal liver function; for chronic use or older adults consider limiting to ≤ 3 g/day. Count combination opioid–acetaminophen products and OTC sources toward the daily total. Use with caution with immunotherapy (possible reduced efficacy) and where fever-masking is a concern. PAIN-E 1 of 2 Use with caution — many patients with cancer are at high risk for renal, GI, cardiac, bleeding or thrombocytopenia toxicity, amplified by concurrent chemotherapy (especially angiogenesis inhibitors). Use the shortest duration and lowest effective dose. Ibuprofen 400–800 mg 4×/day (daily maximum 3200 mg) Naproxen 220–500 mg 2–3×/day (daily maximum 1500 mg) Ketorolac 15–30 mg IV every 6 h, short-term only — maximum 5 days Celecoxib (COX-2) up to 200 mg twice daily; does not inhibit platelet aggregation Topical diclofenac gel 1% 4×/day, solution 2% 4×/day, or patch 1.3% 1–2 patches/day — for peripheral joint pain, reduced systemic absorption Monitor blood pressure, renal function, LFTs and CBC at baseline and as indicated. Avoid oral NSAIDs during prophylactic/therapeutic anticoagulation; celecoxib or a topical NSAID may be options. Stop the NSAID if heart failure/hypertension or hepatic or GI toxicity develops. PAIN-E 1 of 2 / 2 of 2 Adjuvant analgesics for neuropathic pain Antidepressants and anticonvulsants are first-line adjuvants for cancer-related neuropathic pain and are often combined with an opioid. Titrate to effect; failure of one agent in a class does not predict failure of the class. Anticonvulsants Gabapentin Start 100–300 mg nightly; increase to 900–3600 mg/day in 2–3 divided doses (increments of 50%–100% every ~3 days). Slower titration and renal dose-adjustment as needed. Anticonvulsants Pregabalin Start 50–75 mg nightly → twice daily, increments of 50%–100% every 3 days to a maximum 600 mg/day. Renal dose-adjustment; better GI absorption than gabapentin. Antidepressants (SNRI) Duloxetine Start 20–30 mg daily; after 1 week increase to 60 mg/day as tolerated (up to 120 mg for mood). Has data for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy. Antidepressants (SNRI) Venlafaxine ER Start 37.5 mg daily; increase every 4 days to 75–225 mg/day (≥ 150 mg/day needed for SNRI analgesia). Antidepressants (TCA) Nortriptyline / Desipramine Start 10–25 mg nightly; increase every 5–7 days to 50–150 mg nightly. Secondary amines better tolerated; caution with QTc/conduction disease and in older adults. Topical Lidocaine 5% patch Apply daily to the painful site; minimal systemic absorption. Corticosteroid Dexamethasone Once daily in the morning (long half-life, less mineralocorticoid effect). Useful in a pain crisis when neural structures or bone are involved; significant long-term adverse effects — taper case-by-case. Check for serotonergic drug interactions (serotonin-syndrome risk). Some SSRIs/SNRIs may reduce tamoxifen activation. PAIN-F 1 of 2 / 2 of 2 Equianalgesic doses & opioid rotation Single-dose equivalences relative to morphine — estimates only; institutional variation applies. Use to convert or rotate opioids, not as fixed prescribing doses. Morphine 10 mg 30 mg 3–4 h Hydromorphone 1.5 mg 7.5 mg 2–3 h Fentanyl 100 mcg acute (250 mcg chronic) — see patch Oxycodone — 20 mg 3–5 h Hydrocodone — 30 mg 3–5 h Oxymorphone — 10 mg 4–6 h Levorphanol — 4 mg 6–8 h Codeine — 200 mg 3–4 h Tramadol — 300 mg 6 h Tapentadol — 100 mg 6–8 h Methadone and buprenorphine conversions are specialist-only and are not reduced to a single ratio. Total the current opioid over 24 h and calculate the equianalgesic dose of the new opioid. If pain was controlled and the patient is opioid-tolerant, reduce by 25%–50% for incomplete cross-tolerance; if the previous opioid was ineffective, begin at 100% of the equianalgesic dose. Provide breakthrough doses of 10%–20% of the total daily dose; account for renal/hepatic impairment. Transdermal fentanyl is only for opioid-tolerant patients with relatively stable pain (not for rapid titration). Conversion ratio ~200 mg/day oral morphine ≈ 100 mcg/h patch (i.e. ~2 mg/day oral morphine ≈ 1 mcg/h), rounded down for incomplete cross-tolerance; patches come in 12, 25, 50, 75 and 100 mcg/h. Heat/fever can accelerate absorption. Provide a short-acting opioid for breakthrough. Not recommended for cancer pain: meperidine (CNS-toxic metabolite normeperidine) and mixed agonist–antagonists (pentazocine, nalbuphine, butorphanol) — which can precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients. PAIN-G 10 of 22 (Table 2) / 11 of 22 / 12 of 22 / 13 of 22 Managing opioid adverse effects Anticipate and treat adverse effects aggressively. Most improve over time — constipation does not. If they persist, consider opioid rotation. Start a prophylactic stimulant laxative with every opioid — senna 2 tablets daily (FDA-recommended maximum 8 tablets/day), and/or polyethylene glycol 17 g in 8 oz water 1–2×/day; increase the laxative as the opioid dose rises. If it persists, add magnesium hydroxide 30–60 mL daily, bisacodyl 5–15 mg PO daily (or 10 mg suppository PR), or lactulose 30–60 mL daily, and consider a PAMORA (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, or naldemedine). Rule out obstruction; rectal suppositories/enemas are contraindicated in neutropenia or thrombocytopenia. Prochlorperazine 10 mg PO every 6 h PRN; metoclopramide 10–15 mg PO 4×/day PRN; or haloperidol 0.5–1 mg PO every 6–8 h PRN. Alternatives include ondansetron 4–8 mg or olanzapine 2.5–5 mg at bedtime. Opioid-induced nausea often resolves with continued use; if it persists beyond ~1 week, reassess and consider opioid rotation. Rule out other causes. If opioid-related, give a lower dose more frequently, or reduce the dose if pain control holds. A CNS stimulant may be added — caffeine 100–200 mg PO every 6 h, or methylphenidate 5–10 mg 1–3×/day (morning/early afternoon to avoid insomnia). Sedation typically precedes respiratory depression; a respiratory rate < 10/min is an early sign. For reversal in an unstable patient: dilute one ampule of naloxone (0.4 mg/1 mL) into 9 mL normal saline (total 10 mL) and give 1–2 mL (0.04–0.08 mg) every 30–60 s until improvement; be ready to repeat, as the opioid half-life outlasts naloxone. Consider a naloxone infusion after a long-acting or sustained-release opioid. PAIN-H 1 of 3 / 2 of 3 / 3 of 3 NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology (NCCN Guidelines®), Adult Cancer Pain, Version 2.2026. © National Comprehensive Cancer Network. All recommendations category 2A unless otherwise indicated.
